newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-'OUTSIDER' TOMBA READY TO SPRING SURPRISE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-'OUTSIDER' TOMBA READY TO SPRING SURPRISE.

text.p: If Alberto Tomba is in the top five or six after the first leg of Wednesday's giant slalom at the Alpine skiing world championships, his rivals had better watch out.

Although Tomba failed to finish the only giant slalom he has entered this winter in Kranjska Gora, thereby losing his place in the group of top 15 seeds, the Italian is convinced he can cause a surprise.
"People will be amazed at the level of my giant slalom," said the defending champion, who has been training intensively at Corno alle Scale near his native Bologna.
"I am in a better position than last year because I don't have the pressure to do well," he said.

The 30-year-old Tomba may believe that, although he can hardly ignore the pressure of competing at home before thousands of fans, the expectations are certainly lower -- at least for the giant slalom if not Saturday's slalom.
As in 1987 when Tomba clinched his first World Cup win as a 20-year-old with start number 25 on the Kandahar piste in Sestriere, he will go into Wednesday's race as an outsider.
"At 10 o'clock in the morning the piste should be hard and icy, so it should be possible for me to get into the top five after the first leg despite a high start number," he said.
"Then my rivals know what I am capable of doing in the second run."
'La Bomba' missed the first few races of the season due to a knee and a wrist injury sustained in a heavy fall during training, while a bout of influenza slowed him down in early January.
However, he gave his confidence a boost by clinching the night slalom in Schladming two weeks ago for his 48th career World Cup victory.
"I will be happy with any medal, especially with the silver which is still missing from my collection," said Tomba, who took giant slalom bronze at his first world championships in 1987.
But his rivals have medal ambitions, too.

Michael Von Gruenigen, the Swiss leader of the giant slalom World Cup standings, will be chasing the first gold medal of his career after collecting two bronzes at last year's world championships in Spain's Sierra Nevada.
"I have achieved my main goals of the winter. I won Alta Badia and Kranjska Gora for the first time and have good chances of winning the giant slalom crystal globe.
"Now it's up to me to get the gold everyone expected me to win in Sierra Nevada," said Von Gruenigen.
After his victory in Kranjska Gora, the Swiss said: "Tomba will be ready for Sestriere. I am surprised at how strong he skied the first leg."
Strong competition will also come from Norway's Kjetil Andre Aamodt, the overall World Cup leader who edged Von Gruenigen for victory in Adelboden and twice finished third.
Aamodt is oozing confidence after picking up the 11th medal of his career when he won last Thursday's combined.
Austria's hopes lie with Hans Knauss, third in the giant slalom standings behind Von Gruenigen and Aamodt.
He said he would rather crash out than finish fourth again as he did in the super-G.
"However, that fourth place showed me I could be fast again," said Knauss, whose form had wavered due to fatigue in January following a fantastic start to the season.
Josef Strobl, the only Austrian to have won a giant slalom this season, lost his place in the team to Andreas Schifferer after crashing out of Saturday's downhill.
Schifferer, who was third in Adelboden, was also a last minute qualifier for the downhill team over Hannes Trinkl, and he finished that race in fifth place.
Other favourites include Fredrik Nyberg of Sweden, Switzerland's 1996 silver medallist Urs Kaelin and compatriot Steve Locher, who won the season's opener in Soelden.
